title: Is the Pin-Prick Worth It?
html:
Good morning,

Napoleon Bonaparte said:

“If they want peace, nations should avoid the pin-pricks that precede cannon shots.”

The same goes for any relationship.

Most relationships are not damaged by one enormous event. The trouble often starts much smaller.

A sarcastic remark.
An unnecessary correction.
A joke with a sharp edge.
A tiny dig made because you are tired, irritated or want to score a point.

One comment might not seem like much.

But then comes another.

And another.

Each one leaves a tiny wound. Each one adds a little more resentment and, eventually, someone has had enough and fires back.

The cannon goes off. Boom!

Now you are no longer arguing about that comment. You are arguing about every comment that came before it.

This happens in marriages, families, friendships and workplaces.

We tell ourselves we are only joking. We might even say the other person is too sensitive.

We defend the pin-prick while ignoring the damage it was designed to do.

Because, if we are honest, many of these comments are not harmless. They are small attempts to punish, provoke or win.

And what do we win?

A brief moment of satisfaction at the expense of trust, peace and connection.

This does not mean avoiding difficult conversations. If something matters, talk about it. Be honest. Be direct.

But do it to resolve the issue, not to wound the person.

Peace is not created by pretending nothing is wrong. It is created by refusing to turn every irritation into an attack.

Before you speak, pause.

Ask yourself:

Am I trying to improve this relationship, or am I simply trying to win a point?

This Week’s MondayMotivator

Avoid the pin-pricks that precede cannon shots.

You do not have to say everything that comes into your head. Sometimes protecting the relationship is more important than winning the moment.

Prompt for the Week

What small comments, jibes or digs have I been making, and what might happen if I stopped?

To your success!

Glenn
